## Does anything actually treat infant colic?

**TL;DR** — Colic is common, has no established cause, and resolves on its own by month three to four. One probiotic strain buys breastfed babies about 25 minutes less crying a day; the largest trial found no benefit at all, and every other common remedy fails its tests. The strongest intervention is supporting the parents until it passes.

### Colic is common, defined by a stopwatch, and ends on its own

- The classic definition is the "rule of threes": crying or fussing ≥3 hours a day, ≥3 days a week, for ≥3 weeks in a healthy, thriving infant [Gutiérrez-Castrellón et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1097/md.0000000000009375).
- The Rome IV criteria drop the stopwatch: prolonged, unexplained crying in a thriving infant [Benninga et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.016).
- The two most rigorous community surveys put cumulative incidence at 5–19%, with no link to sex, social class, or feeding type [Lucassen 2001](https://doi.org/10.1136/adc.84.5.398).
- Crying peaks around week six and fades by month three to four in virtually all infants, treated or not [Gutiérrez-Castrellón et al. 2017](https://doi.org/10.1097/md.0000000000009375), [Hjern et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1111/apa.15247).

### The cause is unknown; the gut is the prime suspect

- No mechanism is established; gas, temperament, and parenting were never convicted [Zeevenhooven et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41575-018-0008-7).
- Colicky infants show raised faecal calprotectin and fewer *Bifidobacterium* whatever their feeding mode [Rhoads et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpeds.2018.07.042).
- Baseline gut-bacteria composition partly predicts which infants will still be crying a month later [Loughman et al. 2021](https://doi.org/10.1017/s2040174420000227).
- Children who were colicky babies have five- to six-fold higher odds of later migraine — some colic may be an early pain syndrome [Gelfand et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.1177/0333102414534326).

### One probiotic strain helps — but only breastfed babies

- Pooled individual data from four double-blind trials: −25.4 min/day crying at day 21, number needed to treat 2.6 in breastfed infants [Sung et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2017-1811).
- The largest, strictest trial (167 infants, first to include formula-fed): no benefit, and 49 min/day *more* fussing [Sung et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.g2107).
- European guidance now recommends the strain for breastfed colicky infants only, and nothing for formula-fed ones [Szajewska et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.1097/mpg.0000000000003633).
- [Figure 1](#fig-colic-treatments) plots the three verdicts side by side.

**Figure 1. The best treatment helps some babies — and failed its biggest test.**
- **Shows:** Reported change in daily crying/fussing versus placebo for the pooled probiotic trials, the largest single trial, and pooled lactase trials.
- **Evidence boundary:** Different populations and feeding modes — three separate verdicts, not one pooled effect.
- **Sources:** [Sung et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2017-1811), [Sung et al. 2014](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.g2107), [Kozłowska‐Jalowska et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1002/jpn3.12144)

### Everything else fails its tests

- Simethicone (gas drops): no benefit over placebo; proton pump inhibitors: not supported [Ellwood et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-035405).
- Dietary changes (hydrolysed formula, low-allergen maternal diet): low-quality evidence only [Gordon et al. 2018](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd011029.pub2).
- Lactase drops: no significant effect in pooled trials [Kozłowska‐Jalowska et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1002/jpn3.12144).
- Chiropractic and osteopathic manipulation: the effect disappears in parent-blinded trials [Dobson et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.cd004796.pub2).

### The real burden lands on parents — and it ends

- Inconsolable crying quadruples the odds of maternal depressive symptoms at two months [Radesky et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2012-3316).
- In a survey of 3,259 families, 5.6% of parents admitted smothering, slapping, or shaking their baby because of crying [Reijneveld et al. 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/s0140-6736%2804%2917191-2).
- Long-term outcomes show associations only — more adolescent indigestion-type complaints, no proven lasting harm [Zeevenhooven et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1111/apa.17215), [Indrio et al. 2023](https://doi.org/10.3390/nu15030615).
- Every guideline starts with parental reassurance, not a prescription [Ellwood et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-035405).
